description: Hi! I'm Jason Ou, a Babson College student studying Applied AI. I teach AI literacy to non-technical learners, from families to kids in rural Yunnan, China. For the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, I'm building a browser game where kids ages 7 to 12 run a Moon outpost and balance power, oxygen, and radiation shielding using real NASA space weather data. Looking for teammates into game design, HTML/JavaScript, or illustration.
summary: BOLT: 5 Days on the Moon is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. A real-style solar storm has injured Commander Kai at a Moon base near the lunar south pole. The player is BOLT, the base's helper robot, and must keep Kai alive for 5 days until a rescue ship arrives. Kids balance three resources (power, air, and radiation shielding) while dust, loose cables, leaks, and frozen batteries break the base in animated pixel scenes. BOLT can only do 3 jobs per day, and every job costs something, so there is never a free safe choice. Repairs are hands-on mini games: kids drag a plug back into its socket, rub dust off panels, swap filters, patch leaks, stack Moon-soil bags, and crank a heater. Solar storms in the game come from real NASA DONKI records, and the ending shows which real storms the player survived.
details:
What it does:

- Opens with a 4-part pixel story based on the real solar storm of August 4, 1972, which happened between Apollo 16 and Apollo 17. In the game, Commander Kai is caught outside, gets hurt, and the storm damages the base.

- The player is BOLT, a robot who has to make the decisions while the commander rests. Kai sometimes wakes up to give hints, and the player can wake Kai on purpose, but that costs Kai some health.

- The base is shown as a cross-section with 5 areas: solar panels, radiation shield, oxygen machine, battery, and med bay. Problems are animated: dust covers the panels, a loose cable sparks, the air pipe sprays gas, the filter smokes, battery cells go dark, and the shield cracks glow red.

- Each day BOLT can do only 3 jobs. Every job also costs power, air, health, or a medicine pack. Outdoor repairs cost air because the airlock lets air escape.

- Repairs are hands-on mini games with the mouse or a finger: drag the loose plug into its socket, rub Moon dust off the panel, pull out the dirty air filter and slide in a clean one, drag a patch onto a leaking pipe and press it down, drag Moon-soil bags into glowing shield cracks, and spin a crank to thaw a frozen battery.

- At night, a new random problem appears, and BOLT sometimes faces a choice alone, with costs on both sides. Every game is different.

- Solar storm warnings show up on the base monitor one day ahead. Each storm is a real NASA DONKI event (for example the X9.3 flare of September 6, 2017). When it hits, the screen turns red and particles rain down, and any that get through the shield damage Kai. Moving Kai to the storm shelter blocks more radiation but hurts Kai's injured leg.

- Chiptune background music, made in code, changes with the situation: a calm base theme, an upbeat repair theme, a tense storm-alert theme, a fast storm theme, a quiet night theme, and win and lose themes. Sound effects play for footsteps, repairs, alarms, and a heartbeat warning when Kai is weak.

- After 5 days a rescue ship lands in an animated ending: the rescue crew walks into the base, Kai gets up, and everyone flies home. The player gets a rank, and the game lists the real storms they survived along with the data sources.

Why it matters: Real missions are about trade-offs. Kids learn that space has no air and no radiation protection, that every repair has a cost, and that space weather is real and can be forecast.

How it works: A single HTML page using an HTML5 Canvas, with all pixel art, music, and sound effects generated in code. It runs in any modern browser with no download and no sign-up.

Use of AI: The game idea and design decisions came from our team. The code (including the code that draws the pixel art and makes the music) was written with AI help (Claude by Anthropic, through Claude Code).
dataRefs: NASA DONKI space weather database (6 real solar flares and CMEs, 2011 to 2024)
NASA Artemis program (lunar south pole setting)
NASA Moon science (lunar night, temperature, Moon dust)
NASA human spaceflight standards (NASA-STD-3001, radiation limit)
projectRefs: Game source code and demo video (GitHub)
Claude by Anthropic via Claude Code (AI help with code and English text)
